analogy.p: The pump is the cell: it gives the water energy. The water flowing round the pipes is the current. The pressure difference across a radiator is the potential difference, and a narrow section of pipe is a resistor. The same amount of water flows past every point in a single loop, just as the current is the same everywhere in a series circuit. It breaks down because water leaves a tap and can be stored, whereas in a circuit the charges are already in the wire and are simply pushed round; they are not used up.

bullets: Draw and interpret circuit diagrams using standard symbols.
**Electric current** is a flow of electrical charge; its size is the rate of flow of charge.
Equation: **Q = I t** (charge in coulombs, current in amperes, time in seconds).
In a **single closed loop** the current is the same at any point.
A circuit needs a **complete loop** and a **source of potential difference** for current to flow.
Know how an **ammeter** (series) and a **voltmeter** (parallel) are connected.
This is a foundation for resistance, I-V graphs, series/parallel rules, power and energy.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This spec point is the foundation of the whole Electricity topic. You must be able to **recognise and draw standard circuit symbols**, state that **electric current is the flow of electrical charge**, and know that the size of the current is the **rate of flow of charge**. You must use the equation **charge flow = current x time (Q = I t)** and know that in a **single closed loop the current has the same value at every point**. Almost every later electricity question (resistance, series and parallel, power, energy) assumes you can do these things quickly and without error.

bullets: Current = **rate of flow of electrical charge**.
In metals the carriers are **free electrons**; in electrolytes they are **ions**.
Measured in **amperes (A)**; 1 A means 1 coulomb of charge passes each second.
Small currents are given in milliamperes: 1 mA = 0.001 A.
Electrons drift slowly (millimetres per second) but the effect is almost instant, like pushing a full pipe of water.
Current is **conserved**: the same charge entering a component leaves it.
Insulators have no free charge carriers, so almost no current flows.
core.p: **Electric current** is a flow of electric charge past a point in a circuit. In a metal wire the charge carriers are **free (delocalised) electrons**. These are electrons that are not bound to one atom and can move through the lattice of positive metal ions. In a conducting solution or molten ionic compound the charge carriers are **ions**. The current tells you how much charge passes a point every second, so a larger current means more charge flows each second. Current is **not** used up and electrons do not travel round the circuit at the speed of light; the electrons drift slowly but the whole chain of charges starts to move at once.

bullets: Symbol: Q. Unit: **coulomb (C)**.
1 A = 1 C per second (1 A = 1 C/s).
Charge flow is the **total** amount of charge that moves; current is the **rate**.
Time must always be in **seconds**; convert minutes by multiplying by 60 and hours by 3600.
Current must be in **amperes**; convert mA by dividing by 1000.
Charge is conserved: none is lost in a component.
A larger current moves more charge in the same time.
core.h: Charge, the coulomb and the ampere
core.p: **Electric charge** (symbol **Q**) is measured in **coulombs (C)**. A flow of charge is a current, so the coulomb and ampere are linked: **one ampere is a rate of flow of one coulomb per second**. The more charge that moves, or the longer it flows for, the greater the total charge transferred. Charge is a conserved quantity, which means it can be moved around but not created or destroyed. In this topic you only need to deal with the total charge moved and never with the charge on a single electron.

bullets: **Q = I t**: charge = current x time.
**I = Q / t**: current = charge divided by time.
**t = Q / I**: time = charge divided by current.
Write the equation, then the substitution, then the answer with a unit.
Convert units **first**: 2 minutes = 120 s; 250 mA = 0.25 A.
A graph of Q against t is a straight line through the origin if the current is constant; the **gradient is the current**.
Check the answer is sensible: a bigger current or a longer time must give more charge.
core.h: The equation Q = I t and how to rearrange it
core.p: The equation linking charge, current and time is **charge flow (C) = current (A) x time (s)**, written **Q = I t**. You must learn this equation, because AQA does not give it to you in the exam. Use a triangle with Q at the top and I and t at the bottom, or rearrange algebraically: **I = Q / t** and **t = Q / I**. The most common source of lost marks is forgetting to convert the time to seconds or the current to amperes, so check your units before substituting.

bullets: Closed circuit = **no gaps**; an open switch makes a gap.
A **cell** supplies potential difference; a **battery** is two or more cells connected together.
The p.d. is the energy transferred per unit charge (volts, V).
No p.d. means random motion of electrons only, so no current.
Remember: potential difference is **across** a component; current is **through** it.
Components in the loop transfer the energy to the surroundings.
core.h: Why a closed circuit and a source of potential difference are needed
core.p: For a current to flow, two conditions must be met. First, there must be a **complete (closed) circuit**, because charge can only keep flowing round if there is a continuous conducting path. A break, such as an open switch, stops the flow everywhere. Second, there must be a source of **potential difference (p.d.)**, such as a cell, battery or power supply, which provides the energy to push the charge round. The potential difference is the 'push' and the current is the resulting flow. Without a p.d. the free electrons move randomly and there is no net flow.

bullets: Conventional current: **+ to -** around the external circuit.
Electron flow: **- to +** (opposite direction).
Both describe the same current; the choice is just a convention.
The long line of a cell symbol is the **positive** terminal; the short thick line is negative.
In a diode, conventional current flows in the direction of the triangle arrow.
Always label the direction of current with an arrow on the wire.
A voltmeter branch carries almost no current, so the main current arrow goes along the main loop.
core.p: By **convention**, current is drawn flowing from the **positive terminal** of the cell round the circuit to the **negative terminal**. This is called **conventional current**. Scientists agreed this convention before electrons were discovered. In reality, the negatively charged **electrons** in a metal drift the opposite way, from the negative terminal to the positive terminal. In exam diagrams you almost always use conventional current, so draw arrows from + to - unless the question specifically asks about electron flow.

bullets: Single loop: **I is the same everywhere**.
Reason: charge is conserved, so the flow of charge into a component equals the flow out.
Components do not use up current; they transfer **energy**.
Identical ammeter readings in the loop prove this.
The potential difference is **shared** between components in series; the current is not.
If one component breaks the loop, current stops everywhere.
Branches (parallel) are different and are covered in the series and parallel topic.
core.h: Same current everywhere in a single closed loop
core.p: In a circuit with only one loop (a series circuit), the **current is the same at every point**. An ammeter placed before the lamp, after the lamp or anywhere else in the loop will give the same reading. This happens because charge cannot be stored or lost: for every coulomb that enters a component, one coulomb leaves. What does change is the **energy** carried by each coulomb, because the components transfer energy to the surroundings. A common wrong idea is that the lamp 'uses up' current. It uses up **energy** and the charge carries on round.

bullets: **Cell**: one long thin line (+) and one short thick line (-).
**Battery**: two or more cells in series.
**Switch**: open (gap) or closed (joined).
**Fixed resistor**: a rectangle; **variable resistor**: rectangle with an arrow through it.
**Filament lamp**: a circle with a cross.
**Fuse**: a rectangle with a line through it.
**Diode**: a triangle pointing along conventional current, with a bar; **LED**: a diode in a circle with arrows leaving.
**Thermistor**: resistor with a hooked diagonal line; **LDR**: resistor in a circle with arrows pointing in.
**Ammeter**: circle with A; **voltmeter**: circle with V.
core.h: Standard circuit symbols you must recognise
core.p: Examiners expect you to recognise the symbols and to draw them neatly with a ruler. Learn the shape and the name of each. The tricky pairs are the **cell and battery**, the **diode and LED**, and the **thermistor and LDR**. Wires are drawn as straight lines with corners that are square, and gaps are only left where a component sits.

bullets: Use a **ruler** and make wires straight with right-angled corners.
Keep a **complete loop**.
Place the ammeter in **series** in the main loop.
Place the voltmeter in **parallel** across the component only.
Label components if the question asks (for example R or lamp).
Do not put a voltmeter in the main loop.
Switches are normally drawn in the main loop so they control the whole circuit.
core.p: A good circuit diagram is neat, uses the standard symbols and shows a complete loop. Mark schemes award separate marks for the correct components, the correct positions of the ammeter and voltmeter, and a complete circuit with no gaps. Use a ruler, make corners square and do not draw wires through symbols. Where the question says 'draw a circuit to measure the resistance', include a cell, the component under test, an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel.

bullets: Ammeter: **series**, measures current (A).
Voltmeter: **parallel**, measures p.d. (V).
The ammeter has a **very low resistance**; the voltmeter has a **very high resistance**.
Connect the positive terminal of the meter towards the positive side of the cell.
If a voltmeter were in series it would almost stop the current.
Take readings with the circuit switched on only briefly to prevent heating of wires.
Read the scale carefully and use the correct units.
core.h: Using an ammeter and a voltmeter
core.p: An **ammeter** measures the **current through a component** and must be connected in **series**, so that the same current flows through it. A **voltmeter** measures the **potential difference across a component** and must be connected in **parallel** with it. An ideal ammeter has very low resistance so it does not change the current; an ideal voltmeter has very high resistance so it takes almost no current. These meters are used in the required practicals on resistance.

bullets: Axes: Q (C) on y, t (s) on x.
Constant current gives a **straight line through the origin**.
**Gradient = I = change in Q / change in t**.
Use a large triangle for accuracy, and show the dashed lines.
Steeper line: larger current.
Horizontal line: no current is flowing.
Area under an I against t graph gives charge (extension).
core.h: Reading and drawing Q against t graphs
core.p: If a constant current flows, the charge transferred grows steadily with time, so a graph of **charge (y-axis) against time (x-axis)** is a straight line through the origin. Because I = Q / t, the **gradient** of the line equals the **current**. A steeper line means a larger current. If the line is curved, the current is changing, and the gradient at any point gives the current at that moment. In an exam you may be asked to find the current from the gradient: take a large triangle, read the change in Q and the change in t, then divide.

bullets: Resistance: **V = I R**.
Energy: **E = Q V**, and **E = P t**.
Power: **P = I V** and **P = I squared R**.
Series and parallel: current splits at junctions in parallel, as charge is conserved.
Metallic bonding (Chemistry): free delocalised electrons carry the charge.
Static electricity: charge builds up when electrons transfer between insulators.
Mains electricity: the a.c. current changes direction, unlike d.c. from cells.
core.p: These ideas are used again and again in physics. Potential difference is linked to energy by **E = QV**, so the charge you calculate here appears in the energy transfer calculations. Current and p.d. give resistance through **V = I R**. The rules for series and parallel circuits rely on the conservation of charge. Power is calculated using **P = I V**. The idea that the metal has free electrons links to the chemistry of metallic bonding, and the idea of an electric field links to static electricity.

exam: **Calculation (3 marks)**: 1 mark for the correct equation, 1 for substitution (with correct units), 1 for the answer with unit.
Always convert **minutes to seconds** and **mA to A** before substituting; this is a favourite trap.
**Describe**: current is the rate of flow of charge; use this exact phrase for definition questions (1 mark).
**Circuit drawing (3-4 marks)**: correct symbols, complete loop, ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel across the component.
Draw with a **ruler**; untidy, gapped or curved wires can lose marks.
For 'explain why the ammeter readings are the same' write: charge is conserved, so the **same current** flows at every point in a single loop.
Use 'potential difference' rather than 'voltage' in an explanation, although 'voltage' is accepted in everyday language.
Graph questions: read the gradient of Q against t as the current; show the triangle and give the unit (A).
Give final answers with the correct unit and a sensible number of significant figures.
When asked to 'suggest' a reason, apply the conservation of charge idea rather than 'it gets used up'.
Check direction: draw the current arrows from + to - on the diagram.

mistakes.r: Current is the **same** before and after the lamp; the **energy** is transferred.
mistakes.w: Current is used up by the lamp.

mistakes.r: **Conventional current** is + to -; electrons actually drift from - to +.
A voltmeter goes in **parallel** across the component; an ammeter goes in series.
**Q = I t**; rearranged I = Q / t and t = Q / I.
Convert time to **seconds** and current to **amperes** first.
mistakes.w: Using minutes or milliamperes straight into the equation.

mistakes.r: Charge (C) is the quantity; current (A) is the **rate** of flow of charge.
mistakes.w: Charge and current are the same thing.

mistakes.r: A cell has a **long thin** line (+) and a **short thick** line (-).
mistakes.w: Draw a cell as two lines of equal length.

mistakes.r: A **battery** is two or more cells connected together.
mistakes.w: A battery is a single cell.

mistakes.r: The cell gives energy to the charges; the electrons are already in the wire.

summary: You need to know the standard circuit symbols, that electric current is the rate of flow of electrical charge, and how to use Q = I t, including the fact that the current is the same everywhere in a single closed loop. These ideas underpin every later electricity topic, so they must be secure and quick to apply.

terms.d: The rate of flow of electrical charge.
A property of matter measured in coulombs (C); a flow of charge makes a current.
The unit of electric charge; the charge transferred when a current of 1 A flows for 1 s.
The unit of electric current; a flow of 1 coulomb of charge per second.
The total amount of charge that passes a point, Q = I t.
The direction of current drawn from the positive terminal to the negative terminal.
An electron in a metal that is not attached to one atom and is free to move.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points, measured in volts (V).
A source of potential difference that uses a chemical reaction.
Two or more cells connected together.
A complete loop of conductors that allows current to flow.
A circuit with a single loop, so the current is the same at every point.
A meter connected in series that measures current in amperes.
A meter connected in parallel that measures potential difference in volts.
A safety device that melts and breaks the circuit when the current is too large.
A component that allows current in only one direction.
Light emitting diode: a diode that gives out light when current flows through it.
A resistor whose resistance changes with temperature.
Light dependent resistor: a resistor whose resistance changes with light intensity.
